clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive chorioretinal dystrophy caused by variants in CHM, encoding Rab escort protein 1 (REP1), affecting males
Presents in boys or young men with night blindness followed by progressive peripheral (ring) visual field constriction
Fundus shows progressive, scalloped atrophy of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium, exposing underlying sclera
Central vision is typically preserved until relatively late, distinguishing it from many macular dystrophies
Carrier females are usually asymptomatic but characteristically show a patchy, mottled pigmentary fundus from X-inactivation mosaicism
Autofluorescence and OCT clearly delineate the preserved central island, useful for prognosis and trial monitoring
It is a leading target for retinal gene therapy given its monogenic X-linked basis
reference.pathophysiology: Choroideremia is caused by loss of function of REP1, a protein that escorts Rab GTPases for prenylation, a lipid modification essential for intracellular vesicular trafficking. Although a related protein partly compensates elsewhere, the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptors, and choroid are particularly dependent on REP1, so deficiency impairs their vesicle transport and membrane function. This leads to progressive degeneration of the photoreceptor-retinal pigment epithelium-choriocapillaris complex, beginning in the periphery and advancing centrally, with characteristic loss of the choroid exposing bare sclera. The X-linked pattern reflects the gene's location, with mosaic expression producing the milder carrier fundus.
additionalDifferentials: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina
additionalInvestigations: Fundus autofluorescence to map the residual central island and rate of loss
Optical coherence tomography of macular structure and photoreceptor preservation
Electroretinography documenting rod-predominant then generalised dysfunction
Automated perimetry to track peripheral field constriction
Examination of carrier relatives for the characteristic mottled fundus
redFlags: Encroachment of atrophy on the central macular island threatening acuity
Development of macular oedema or complications compromising residual vision
Atypical features suggesting an alternative chorioretinal dystrophy
reference.prognosis: It is a slowly progressive disorder in which night blindness and peripheral field loss advance over decades, with central acuity often preserved until middle age before eventual severe visual impairment; gene therapy trials aim to slow or halt degeneration.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as retinitis pigmentosa and missing the specific X-linked genetic basis and therapeutic implications
Overlooking the carrier fundus in the mother, which supports the diagnosis and guides counselling
Assuming poor central vision early, when the central island is usually retained until late
Failing to consider eligibility for gene-therapy trials in suitable patients
